network.overall_strategy: Build methional by methanethiol addition to acrolein, then introduce the amino-acid carbon through Strecker chemistry. Ten graph-distinct pathways combine two acrolein sources, three experimentally supported but unequally effective methanethiol sources, and two terminal processing sequences. These are not ten independently demonstrated prebiotic syntheses: the discharge-fed Strecker framework is the experimental reference; the other combinations join separately demonstrated modules, and the hydantoin branches have preparative rather than integrated prebiotic support. Unsupported sulfur-nitrile photoreduction and enzyme-dependent methylation are excluded. Competing sulfide addition, reversible cyanohydrin formation, and thermal decarboxylation are explicitly represented. All environments are anoxic; surface reaction pools require local UV shielding, not an ozone layer. Numerical conditions explicitly labeled proposed are experimental screening specifications, not literature measurements or demonstrated geological conditions. Transport equations and survival thresholds identify measurements needed to establish productive flux; they do not supply missing rate constants or establish natural viability. Discharge reactions are atom-balanced aggregate production channels, not elementary mechanisms or independent yield predictions. Neutral molecular formulas provide reference-species bookkeeping; aqueous protonation and counterions depend on the stated pH. A null environment_formed denotes an external feedstock or, for methanethiol, formation in multiple environments. Because the schema has no coproduct or sink role, those species use intermediate without implying productive participation.

reactions.name: Discharge production and aqueous collection of formaldehyde

conditions.temperature: 300-370 K bulk gas and collection water; the electrical-discharge channel is nonthermal and locally much hotter
conditions.other: Anoxic gas-water discharge system. A reported reference mixture contained CH4 258, CO2 87, H2S 100 and NH3 250 mm Hg, with 300 mL water, approximately 3 days of discharge and final solution pH near 8. These are laboratory reference conditions, not a reconstructed global atmosphere. Collect water-soluble products continuously into 300-323 K water. Atmospheric collection efficiency and dilution must be measured separately.

reactions.mechanism: Aggregate plasma-driven carbon and oxygen radical chemistry produces formaldehyde; hydrogen closes the net elemental balance. Hydrated formaldehyde in water is represented by its neutral carbonyl reference species.
reactions.reasoning: The supplied review identifies formaldehyde among the discharge-derived precursor pool associated with the methionine framework (Van Trump and Miller, 1972; Parker et al., 2011). This net equation does not establish a single elementary mechanism or a formaldehyde-specific yield. Strongly reducing gas mixtures are most defensible as local scenarios, not an assumed global atmosphere.

reactions.name: Discharge production and aqueous collection of acetaldehyde

conditions.temperature: 300-370 K bulk gas; collect condensate at 300-323 K
conditions.other: Use the approximately 3-day anoxic reducing-discharge reference described in rxn_001. This is a coproduct channel of the same discharge mixture, not an independently optimized selective reactor. Quantify acetaldehyde in both gas and collected liquid; an open evaporating pool cannot be assigned the retention of a closed laboratory apparatus.

reactions.mechanism: Aggregate discharge chemistry couples carbon fragments and introduces oxygen derived from water, producing acetaldehyde and hydrogen.
reactions.reasoning: Acetaldehyde belongs to the precursor inventory discussed for sulfur-containing discharge mixtures and supplies the C2 partner for acrolein formation (Parker et al., 2011; Cleaves, 2003). The balanced aggregate is bookkeeping for a complex mixture, not evidence of selective methane-to-acetaldehyde conversion.

reactions.name: Discharge production of hydrogen cyanide

conditions.temperature: 300-370 K bulk gas; 300-323 K collection water
conditions.other: Anoxic reducing discharge for approximately 3 days using the reference mixture in rxn_001. Collect HCN into the aqueous precursor reservoir. Proposed downstream screening range: 0.1-10 mM total cyanide at pH 8-9, explicitly not a measured rainout concentration. At these pH values substantial cyanide remains volatile HCN, so measure headspace partitioning and losses.

reactions.mechanism: Electrical energy drives carbon-nitrogen radical chemistry and dehydrogenation, represented by a net methane-ammonia-to-HCN channel.
reactions.reasoning: HCN supplies the carboxyl carbon in the supported methional-Strecker framework (Van Trump and Miller, 1972; Parker et al., 2011). Its simultaneous production in laboratory mixtures does not demonstrate environmentally sustained millimolar accumulation.

reactions.name: Direct discharge production of acrolein

conditions.temperature: 300-370 K bulk gas; immediately collect products at 300-323 K
conditions.other: Approximately 3-day reducing-discharge reference as in rxn_001. Proposed collection-water screening pH: 7.5-9. Acrolein must be measured during production rather than inferred from a final accumulated inventory because it reacts rapidly with sulfide, thiols, ammonia and cyanide. No acrolein-specific residence time or yield is supplied by the research synopsis.

reactions.mechanism: Aggregate discharge-driven carbon-chain assembly and oxygen incorporation generate an unsaturated C3 aldehyde.
reactions.reasoning: Acrolein was identified as a discharge product in the methionine synthesis framework (Van Trump and Miller, 1972, as discussed by Parker et al., 2011). This is the reference acrolein source, but the graph does not imply that its complicated plasma mechanism or collection efficiency is established by the balanced net equation.

reactions.name: Discharge production of methanethiol

conditions.temperature: 300-370 K bulk gas; 300-310 K collection water
conditions.other: Use the H2S-bearing, approximately 3-day discharge reference in rxn_001 rather than assuming an unlimited external methanethiol stock. Proposed collection design: gas-to-liquid volume ratio no greater than 0.1 in a covered receiving cavity, with capture time no longer than 1 hour. These are retention-screening assumptions, not demonstrated early-Earth geometry. Measure dissolved and gaseous methanethiol, residual H2S and sulfur-containing side products. Apply the retention equation in rxn_007 with a source-specific capture efficiency.

reactions.mechanism: Discharge-generated methyl and sulfur radicals form methanethiol; the net equation represents a mixture-production channel.
reactions.reasoning: H2S-containing reducing discharges support the methanethiol-dependent route to methionine (Van Trump and Miller, 1972; Parker et al., 2011). Closed-flask production is stronger evidence than an assumed ordinary-vent source, but neither atmospheric abundance nor surface retention is established. The approximately 3 x 10^-3 methionine-to-glycine ratio is a whole-system benchmark, not this reaction's yield.

reactions.name: Dilute crossed aldol formation of acrolein
agents: Hydroxide and general bases supplied by mildly alkaline water

conditions.other: Proposed screen: pH 8.0-9.5, formaldehyde and acetaldehyde each 0.01-1 mM, sampled over 1-30 days under anoxia. These numerical ranges are planning values, not a transcription of Cleaves's protocol. Use covered or optically shielded water and measure acrolein continuously or by frequent sampling. Capture may overlap with rxn_009; acrolein is not assumed to accumulate before use.

reactions.mechanism: Base-promoted acetaldehyde enolization, addition to formaldehyde and dehydration produce acrolein.
reactions.reasoning: Cleaves (2003) demonstrated low but significant steady-state acrolein formation from dilute formaldehyde and acetaldehyde under neutral-to-basic conditions. This provides a chemically distinct alternative to direct discharge acrolein production. Its integration with methanethiol capture and methionine formation has not been demonstrated in one geochemically constrained system.

reactions.name: Molybdenum-sulfide-mediated hydrothermal methanethiol production
agents: Deposited molybdenum sulfide catalyst, nominally MoS2

conditions.pressure: Reported supercritical-CO2 regime; proposed total-pressure screen 100-200 bar, not a quoted experimental pressure
conditions.other: Reported anchors are carbonate-NaCl water, H2, supercritical CO2, 473 K and 14 days. The synopsis does not specify the exact pressure, catalyst loading or medium composition. An explicitly proposed screen is 0.1 M total carbonate, 0.5 M NaCl, 10 mM initial total sulfide, 1 g/L deposited catalyst and an initial H2 partial-pressure target of 20 bar; phase behavior and in-situ pH require measurement. Do not transfer the reported maximum yield to this untested formulation. Proposed export operation: cool the product stream under pressure to at most 323 K within 10 minutes, then collect into an anoxic 300-310 K covered receiving cavity within 1 hour. A retention model is C_delivered = C_source*(V_source/V_capture)*eta_capture*exp(-k_loss*t)/(1+Hcc*V_gas/V_liquid), where Hcc is the effective gas/water concentration ratio. Illustrative acceptance assumptions eta_capture >= 0.5, k_loss <= 0.1 per hour, t <= 1 hour, Hcc <= 1 and V_gas/V_liquid <= 0.1 give retention >= 0.41 before dilution. None of these transport parameters has been measured for the proposed coupled network.

reactions.mechanism: Catalyst-mediated CO2 reduction and sulfur incorporation yield methanethiol, with hydrogen supplying reducing equivalents.
reactions.reasoning: Kitadai et al. (2024) directly demonstrated this source and reported up to 7.9% conversion of supplied H2S to methanethiol after 14 days at 473 K. This does not establish equivalent activity of natural crystalline molybdenite or common FeS-bearing vents. A suitable catalyst-bearing CO2-rich setting and export efficiency remain necessary tests. Reeves et al. (2014) found no evidence for comparable inorganic methanethiol synthesis in the modern vent fluids they examined.

reactions.name: Trace methanethiol production coupled formally to FeS pyritization
agents: Mackinawite FeS as a consumed mineral reactant and reactive surface, not an inert catalyst

conditions.pressure: 20 bar CO2-bearing headspace, proposed screening point
conditions.other: Proposed screen: 14 days, 10 mM initial dissolved total sulfide, 0.1 mol/L solid FeS loading and cooled-sample pH 6-8. These are not claimed to reproduce the original Heinen-Lauwers protocol. Analyze both FeS consumption and pyrite production. Export only the fluid or captured volatile fraction using the cooling, collection and retention accounting in rxn_007; determine a separate source concentration and capture efficiency. With a source yield much below 0.1% of sulfide, 10 mM sulfide supplies much less than 10 micromolar methanethiol before any transport loss. Co-delivered sulfide must remain in the selectivity balance.

reactions.mechanism: A formal net coupling of FeS-to-pyrite conversion with CO2 reduction accounts for reducing equivalents and sulfur incorporation. It is not an assertion that one elementary surface mechanism or the displayed overall mineral conversion was quantitatively established.
reactions.reasoning: Heinen and Lauwers (1996) reported anaerobic alkyl-thiol formation from FeS, H2S and CO2; the methanethiol yield is described as much less than 0.1% of H2S by Kitadai et al. (2024). This is an experimentally grounded but weak supply branch, not a high-yield replacement for the Mo-sulfide system. Natural production and productive export remain unverified (Reeves et al., 2014).

reactions.name: Methanethiol conjugate addition to acrolein

conditions.pressure: 1 atm in a covered collection cavity
conditions.other: Proposed screen: pH 7.5-9.0, acrolein 1-100 micromolar, delivered methanethiol 1-1000 micromolar and 6-72 hours of observation. These are not reported environmental concentrations. Measure sulfide rather than assuming its removal during transfer. An initial selectivity model is f_methional = k_Me*alpha_Me*C_Me/(k_Me*alpha_Me*C_Me + k_HS*alpha_HS*C_sulfide + k_other), with alpha_Me = 1/(1+10^(10.3-pH)) and alpha_HS approximately 1/(1+10^(7.0-pH)) near room temperature. The rate constants and competing pseudo-first-order term k_other are unknown and must be measured. Protect the aqueous reaction locally from direct UV.

reactions.mechanism: Methanethiolate attacks the beta carbon of acrolein; protonation of the resulting enolate produces methional.
reactions.reasoning: This is the defining sulfur-incorporation step proposed for the demonstrated methionine framework and reported to operate even in dilute mixtures (Van Trump and Miller, 1972; Parker et al., 2011). No mineral catalyst is needed. H2S cannot substitute for methanethiol without changing the product: sulfide gives the thiol branch in rxn_017. The coexistence and capture of these volatile reactants remain major bottlenecks.

reactions.name: Reversible formation of the methional imine

conditions.pressure: 1 atm in a covered aqueous reservoir
conditions.other: Proposed screen: pH 8-9, total ammonia 10-100 mM, methional 1-1000 micromolar and sampling over 1 hour to 7 days. These ammonia concentrations require local accumulation and are not assigned to ordinary ocean water. The imine is an equilibrium intermediate trapped by rxn_011, not an assumed isolable stock. If a separate ammonia-rich inflow is invoked, measure its dilution and pH effects.

reactions.mechanism: Ammonia adds to the aldehyde, followed by reversible dehydration of the carbinolamine to an imine or its protonated form.
reactions.reasoning: Imine formation is a mechanistic component of classical methional Strecker synthesis (Barger and Coyne, 1928; Parker et al., 2011). These studies support the overall chemistry, not a measured imine concentration or rate under the proposed dilute screening conditions. Hydrolysis and cyanohydrin formation compete.

reactions.name: Cyanide capture of the methional imine

conditions.pressure: 1 atm in a covered aqueous reservoir
conditions.other: Proposed screen: pH 8-9, total cyanide 0.1-10 mM and total ammonia 10-100 mM, with 6-72 hours of observation while imine formation continues. Determine gas-phase HCN, dissolved cyanide and aminonitrile concentrations. Ammonia and cyanide need not be purified, but losses to residual acrolein and sulfide-containing mixtures must be included.

reactions.mechanism: Cyanide attacks the planar imine or iminium carbon, producing racemic 2-amino-4-(methylsulfanyl)butanenitrile.
reactions.reasoning: Methional-to-methionine Strecker chemistry is experimentally established (Barger and Coyne, 1928; Van Trump and Miller, 1972). Parker et al. (2011) support its relevance to sulfur-bearing discharge mixtures. The product is racemic without an independent stereochemical selection process.

reactions.name: Acid-promoted aminonitrile hydration to methioninamide
agents: Hydronium supplied by a localized acidic volcanic condensate

conditions.other: Proposed screen: nominal 0.1-1 M strong-acid equivalents, pH approximately 0-1 after accounting for incoming alkalinity, sampled from 24 hours to 14 days. This requires an unusually acidic local volcanic-water setting and is not assigned to ordinary ponds. Measure nitrile, amide and free amino acid separately. The acid capacity must accommodate incoming ammonia and other bases. No complete conversion or hydrolysis rate is assumed.

reactions.mechanism: Nitrile protonation enables water addition and tautomerization to the primary amide.
reactions.reasoning: Aminonitrile hydrolysis belongs to the established methional-Strecker synthesis (Barger and Coyne, 1928; Parker et al., 2011). The amide resolves a chemically expected intermediate rather than asserting its isolation in discharge experiments. The specified mild-temperature acidic implementation is a proposed test; the supplied research does not establish its conversion or residence-time requirement.

reactions.name: Methioninamide hydrolysis and release of free methionine
agents: Hydronium supplied by a localized acidic volcanic condensate

conditions.temperature: 363-370 K, followed by cooling to at most 323 K
conditions.other: Proposed screen: pH approximately 0-1 maintained with 0.1-1 M available acid equivalents, observed for 1-14 days. Ammonia is predominantly ammonium under these conditions; neutral formulas are reference-species bookkeeping. Quantify free methionine before any separate analytical forced-hydrolysis treatment. For an illustrative 7-day holding period, retaining at least 80% of already formed methionine requires a measured effective loss constant no greater than 0.00133 per hour. This is an acceptance threshold, not a measured rate. Measure target formation and disappearance in parallel and cool promptly after conversion.

reactions.mechanism: Water attacks the protonated amide carbonyl; cleavage of the carbon-nitrogen bond releases the carboxylic acid and ammonia/ammonium.
reactions.reasoning: The overall Strecker route to methionine is established (Barger and Coyne, 1928; Van Trump and Miller, 1972; Parker et al., 2011). Free amino-acid release under these proposed environmental conditions is nevertheless a kinetic bottleneck. An aminonitrile or amide inventory cannot be counted as accumulated methionine without measuring this conversion and product survival.

reactions.name: Bucherer-Bergs capture of the aminonitrile as methionine hydantoin

conditions.pressure: 1 atm with retained dissolved inorganic carbon
conditions.other: Proposed screen: pH 8-9.5, total inorganic carbon 10-100 mM, total ammonia 10-100 mM, aminonitrile 0.01-1 mM and 1-14 days of observation. CO2 in the net equation represents the incorporated inorganic carbon; bicarbonate and carbonate dominate portions of the aqueous pool. Do not assume industrial conversion at these dilute concentrations.

reactions.mechanism: CO2 capture by the aminonitrile amino group, cyclization involving the nitrile and rearrangement generate the hydantoin ring. There is no net water consumption in this reference-species equation.
reactions.reasoning: The supplied methionine-process literature, including US12187669, supports preparative hydantoin chemistry. Its geochemical implementation at the stated dilute conditions is speculative and is not established by the discharge studies. This branch is retained because it is a real alternative processing chemistry, not because hydantoin formation establishes prebiotic methionine release.

reactions.name: Alkaline hydantoin ring opening to N-carbamoylmethionine
agents: Hydroxide supplied by carbonate-rich alkaline water

conditions.other: Proposed screen: 0.1-0.5 M carbonate alkalinity, cooled-sample pH 10.5-11.5 and residence time 6 hours to 7 days. Determine in-situ hydroxide activity rather than equating hot-fluid pH with the cooled measurement. A proposed natural implementation requires infiltration of hydantoin-bearing water into a confined warm alkaline fracture. Quantify hydantoin recovery during infiltration and adsorption to rock. Cool the outlet to at most 323 K within 10 minutes before transfer to the separate acidic stage in rxn_016. These operations are hypotheses to test, not demonstrated transfers.

reactions.mechanism: Hydroxide-assisted attack at a hydantoin carbonyl opens the ring to an N-carbamoyl amino-acid derivative.
reactions.reasoning: Hydantoin hydrolysis is supported at preparative scale by the supplied methionine-process literature, including US12187669. Conversion at this lower-temperature carbonate-water screen is speculative; industrial performance cannot be transferred to it. Explicitly separating ring opening from decarbamoylation prevents N-carbamoylmethionine from being miscounted as free methionine.

reactions.name: Decarbamoylation and release of methionine
agents: Hydronium supplied by an acidic volcanic-water inflow

conditions.temperature: 363-370 K, proposed screening window; cool product to at most 323 K
conditions.other: After cooling the alkaline stream from rxn_015, mix with a separately characterized acidic inflow. Proposed screen: pH approximately 0-1, residual available acid 0.1-1 M after neutralizing imported carbonate, and 1-14 days of observation. Record dilution, acid demand, carbamoyl-substrate recovery, free methionine, ammonia and inorganic carbon. Apply the measured-survival criterion in rxn_013. If carbamoyl material persists or target loss exceeds release, this branch has not reached the target.

reactions.mechanism: Hydrolysis of the N-carbamoyl group releases the amino acid; the carbamic-acid-derived fragment decomposes to ammonia and CO2.
reactions.reasoning: Preparative conversion of methionine hydantoin to methionine is supported by the supplied process literature, including US12187669, but this staged carbonate-water/acidic-water implementation is speculative. No cited prebiotic experiment establishes complete decarbamoylation under this screening window. The explicit conditions define a falsifiable test rather than resolving the missing kinetic evidence.

reactions.name: Competing sulfide addition to acrolein

conditions.other: Run alongside rxn_009 at pH 7.5-9.0. Proposed sulfide competition screen: 1 micromolar to 10 mM total sulfide, with 6-72 hours of observation and independently varied methanethiol. Measure free 3-mercaptopropanal and secondary sulfur-containing products; the free aldehyde may not accumulate. Use measured branch rates in the selectivity expression of rxn_009.

reactions.mechanism: HS- attacks the beta carbon of acrolein, followed by protonation to produce a terminal thiol rather than a methyl thioether.
reactions.reasoning: Sulfur-addition competition is chemically consistent with the acrolein framework discussed by Cleaves (2003) and Parker et al. (2011). The supplied research does not quantify this specific free-aldehyde sink, so its magnitude is speculative. It is included to prevent the chemically incorrect substitution of H2S for CH3SH in a methionine-producing step; subsequent chemistry would enter homocysteine-type rather than methionine-type precursors.

reactions.name: Reversible trapping of methional as its cyanohydrin

conditions.other: Proposed screen: pH 7-9, total cyanide 0.1-10 mM, variable total ammonia 0-100 mM, and sampling from 1 hour to 7 days. Determine cyanohydrin and aminonitrile separately. The equilibrium constant and forward rate for this mixture are not supplied; do not treat cyanohydrin formation as an irreversible quantitative sink.

reactions.mechanism: Cyanide adds to the aldehyde carbonyl, followed by protonation of the alkoxide to form the cyanohydrin.
reactions.reasoning: Target-specific preparative support is supplied by patent US5705675, which concerns methional and its hydroxynitrile. Its environmental partitioning and rate under this screen are speculative. This competing carbonyl-capture branch is included because the established Strecker framework does not guarantee that every methional molecule forms an aminonitrile.

reactions.name: Cyanohydrin dissociation and return to the methional pool

conditions.other: Observe at pH 7-9 over 1 hour to 7 days, measuring both phases for HCN. Test displacement of the equilibrium by methional consumption in rxn_010, without assuming external cyanide removal. Fit forward and reverse rates jointly with rxn_018. This return edge is not counted as an additional productive pathway.

reactions.mechanism: Reverse cyanohydrin formation regenerates the carbonyl compound and HCN/cyanide pool.
reactions.reasoning: Reversibility follows standard cyanohydrin chemistry, with target-specific preparative context supplied by US5705675. The environmental reverse rate and equilibrium position are speculative because the provided research gives neither. Encoding the return avoids overstating permanent methional loss or inventing an independently demonstrated cyanohydrin-to-methionine route.

reactions.name: Nonoxidative thermal decarboxylation of methionine

conditions.pressure: 100-300 bar, maintaining liquid water throughout the screening range
conditions.other: Anoxic loss control, not a productive-pathway operation. Proposed screening residence times: 0.1-24 hours across cooled-sample pH 5-11. Quantify methionine, the decarboxylation product and additional decomposition products; this single edge is not an exhaustive degradation mechanism. Do not extrapolate dry-state decomposition rates to these fluids. Productive pathways instead cool and retain methionine at the surface.

reactions.mechanism: Thermal decarboxylation removes the amino-acid carboxyl group as CO2 and leaves the corresponding amine.
reactions.reasoning: Li and Brill (2003) provide aqueous hydrothermal context for amino-acid decarboxylation and methionine's limited thermal stability. Yablokov et al. (2009) report dry-state decomposition, which does not supply an aqueous loss constant. The quantitative importance and product selectivity of this sink under the proposed screen remain unmeasured. No O2-dependent oxidation edge is introduced into this anoxic network.

pathways.name: Discharge acrolein and discharge methanethiol through direct Strecker hydrolysis
pathways.description: Reference productive framework: discharge supplies acrolein, methanethiol and HCN; methional formation is followed by Strecker chemistry and hydrolysis. End-to-end laboratory methionine production is supported by Van Trump and Miller (1972) and Parker et al. (2011). The explicitly proposed environmental hydrolysis and collection conditions are not themselves an end-to-end demonstration.

pathways.name: Aldol acrolein and discharge methanethiol through direct Strecker hydrolysis
pathways.description: Discharge-derived formaldehyde and acetaldehyde supply acrolein by the separately demonstrated dilute aldol route. Methanethiol and HCN remain discharge-supplied. This changes the acrolein production chemistry rather than merely reordering reactions. Integrated concentration overlap and free-methionine release remain untested.

pathways.name: Discharge acrolein and Mo-sulfide methanethiol through direct Strecker hydrolysis
pathways.description: Combine discharge acrolein and HCN with the experimentally demonstrated Mo-sulfide methanethiol source. The export operation and retention model are specified in rxn_007, but their efficiencies are unknown. This is a coupled-module hypothesis, not demonstrated hydrothermal methionine synthesis.

pathways.name: Aldol acrolein and Mo-sulfide methanethiol through direct Strecker hydrolysis
pathways.description: Join dilute aldehyde-derived acrolein, captured hydrothermal methanethiol and discharge-derived HCN. Each source has experimental precedent, but neither the export/capture interface nor the full dilute methionine synthesis has been demonstrated. Sulfide competition must be evaluated rather than assuming clean methanethiol delivery.

pathways.name: Discharge acrolein and trace FeS methanethiol through direct Strecker hydrolysis
pathways.description: Use the experimentally reported but very low-yield FeS-associated methanethiol source with discharge acrolein and HCN. Pyrite is a mineral coproduct, not an organic intermediate. Source yield, co-exported sulfide and capture losses may make flux negligible; this pathway is retained as a low-output alternative, not assigned a successful accumulation yield.

pathways.name: Aldol acrolein and trace FeS methanethiol through direct Strecker hydrolysis
pathways.description: Combine the dilute aldol acrolein module with the trace FeS methanethiol module and discharge HCN. This is chemically connected without an unsupported sulfur-methylation step, but productive overlap of two low-abundance precursor streams is unverified. Measured target formation is required before claiming environmental viability.

pathways.name: Discharge precursors through hydantoin capture and staged release
pathways.description: Follow the reference discharge-fed methional and aminonitrile chemistry, then incorporate CO2 to form methionine hydantoin. Alkaline ring opening and separate acidic decarbamoylation replace direct nitrile hydrolysis. The terminal chemistry has preparative precedent, but this staged geological implementation and its release efficiency are speculative.

pathways.name: Aldol acrolein and discharge methanethiol through the hydantoin branch
pathways.description: Aldol-derived acrolein and discharge methanethiol feed the aminonitrile-to-hydantoin alternative. This combines separately supported precursor chemistry with preparative hydantoin chemistry. Neither dilute hydantoin formation nor complete environmental decarbamoylation is established; bound precursor is not counted as methionine.

pathways.name: Discharge acrolein and Mo-sulfide methanethiol through the hydantoin branch
pathways.description: Captured Mo-sulfide-derived methanethiol reacts with discharge acrolein before Strecker and hydantoin processing. Methanethiol generation, warm hydantoin ring opening and acidic target release have independently specified conditions; the 473 K methanethiol-source conditions are not reused for organic assembly. Transfer and release efficiencies remain unmeasured.

pathways.name: Aldol acrolein and Mo-sulfide methanethiol through staged hydantoin processing
pathways.description: Use aldol acrolein, exported Mo-sulfide methanethiol and discharge HCN, then the hydantoin processing branch. This is a distinct combination of real chemical alternatives, not a tenth experimental demonstration. Its multiple unresolved interfaces make it a lower-evidence test case: precursor overlap, catalyst occurrence, retention, ring opening and complete target release all require measurement.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This is the best-supported route, matching the discharge-fed methional/Strecker framework of Van Trump and Miller (1972) and Parker et al. (2011). Its connectivity and net chemistry correctly lead to racemic methionine. The principal unresolved implementation issue is the acidity, temperature and residence time required for rxn_012 and rxn_013. The literature benchmark of approximately 0.003 methionine/glycine supports low-yield production, not a guaranteed yield under unspecified surface conditions.
suggestions: Specify the reducing gas composition, discharge conditions, aqueous collection efficiency and hydrolysis conditions, with reaction-specific references.
Measure free methionine before and after hydrolysis to distinguish environmental production from analytical workup, while quantifying competing sulfide addition and cyanohydrin formation.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Cleaves (2003) supports dilute formaldehyde/acetaldehyde production of a low steady-state acrolein concentration, and the downstream methional/Strecker chemistry is well supported. However, separate demonstrations do not establish sustained methional production in the combined mixture. Acrolein consumption, aldehyde side chemistry and methanethiol loss must be compared with its formation rate. Final hydrolysis remains operationally underspecified.
suggestions: Measure acrolein formation and capture simultaneously in a dilute aldehyde mixture containing realistic ammonia, cyanide and sulfur concentrations.

Provide compatible pH, temperature and residence-time windows for aldol formation, Strecker chemistry and subsequent acid hydrolysis rather than assuming one surface pool supports all steps unchanged.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The methanethiol module has experimental support from Kitadai et al. (2024), but that support is conditional on a specific Mo-sulfide system, including 200 °C operation, supercritical CO2, hydrogen and long reaction times. Connecting its product to the surface Strecker module is chemically credible but not demonstrated. Catalyst availability, cooling/depressurization losses and residual sulfide competition are unresolved. Approval at the pathway cutoff does not establish natural productive flux.
suggestions: Specify the Mo-sulfide phase, loading, geological source, fluid composition, pressure and residence time, distinguishing measured laboratory conditions from proposed natural analogues.
Measure methanethiol recovery through cooling, decompression and transfer, then test the recovered stream directly in methional/Strecker chemistry with its residual sulfide.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Both alternative precursor modules have experimental support, from Cleaves (2003) and Kitadai et al. (2024), and the downstream carbon skeleton is correct. The unresolved issue is whether delivered methanethiol can capture dilute, continuously generated acrolein faster than competing reactions and physical losses. Neither module's isolated yield establishes the combined pathway's throughput. Hydrothermal-to-surface transport and final hydrolysis conditions remain unspecified.
suggestions: Couple a characterized hydrothermal effluent or condensate to the dilute aldol mixture and measure methional, aminonitrile and methionine formation.
Determine actual precursor delivery rates, dilution, residence times and competing-reaction rates instead of multiplying isolated module yields.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Heinen and Lauwers (1996) provide evidence for trace methanethiol formation in FeS/H2S/CO2 systems. The formal pyritization equation is balanced, and trace yield does not make the reaction chemically invalid. However, useful delivery to the acrolein pool is unestablished, particularly in a sulfide-rich mixture that also supports rxn_017. The downstream Strecker route remains sound; uncertainty concerns integrated production and survival rather than the identity of the mineral feedstock.
suggestions: Quantify methanethiol production with isotope tracing, blanks, mineral characterization and sulfur/carbon balances under the proposed conditions.
Measure methanethiol delivery and methional selectivity in the actual sulfide-rich output; retain this branch as a trace-source hypothesis unless productive downstream flux is demonstrated.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This route combines experimentally observed but low-throughput precursor sources. No conservation or carbon-skeleton defect prevents methionine formation. Its main uncertainty is whether trace FeS-derived methanethiol and low steady-state aldol-derived acrolein overlap sufficiently in time and concentration, despite sulfide competition and transport losses. The supplied evidence does not demonstrate that coupling, and the terminal hydrolysis conditions are also missing.
suggestions: Measure both precursor fluxes and their simultaneous capture under realistic dilution and sulfide concentrations.
Use isotope-resolved product analysis to establish that FeS-derived sulfur and inorganic carbon reach methionine, and separately validate the hydrolysis stage.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Bucherer-Bergs capture and hydantoin hydrolysis have preparative support, so this is a chemically legitimate branch rather than an unsupported reaction family. The weak link is the particular staged release scheme: rxn_015 requires a defined alkaline thermal regime, while rxn_016 cannot be assumed to release methionine rapidly merely because N-carbamoylmethionine reaches a surface environment. Nonenzymatic decarbamoylation conditions and product survival need demonstration.
suggestions: Specify ammonia/carbonate activities and hydantoin capture conditions, then establish temperature, pH and residence-time requirements for ring opening and decarbamoylation.
Compare the proposed staged release with complete hydantoin hydrolysis followed by rapid cooling, using measured methionine formation and degradation rates.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The aldol precursor source and preparative hydantoin chemistry are individually credible, but their combination is not an integrated prebiotic demonstration. Productive capture of dilute acrolein is unresolved, and formation of hydantoin or N-carbamoylmethionine alone does not establish target achievement. The principal terminal limitation remains the unspecified nonenzymatic surface decarbamoylation in rxn_016.

evaluation.network_feedback: The network is a credible, literature-aligned synthesis proposal, but it is not APPROVED at the required network threshold of 0.90. Individual pathway flags use the separately requested 0.80 cutoff. Structurally, the 23 molecule nodes and 20 reaction nodes form a connected network with consistent IDs and chemically appropriate routes to DL-methionine. The deterministic balance check is accepted as ground truth: 14 reactions are balanced as written, six require modest coefficients, and none violates atom or charge conservation. Repair the unparsable mol_012 InChI; its stated methional formula is correct, and CSCCC=O is an appropriate connectivity reference. This is a structure-encoding issue, not evidence of an unbalanced reaction. The discharge-fed reference route is experimentally supported, and the network appropriately distinguishes it from combinations of separately demonstrated modules and preparative hydantoin chemistry. FeS-derived methanethiol is not rejected because of its source or low yield alone; its unresolved delivery and competition-limited flux are the concerns. Likewise, Mo-sulfide laboratory results do not establish generic natural vent production, particularly given the modern-fluid findings of Reeves et al. (2014). The supplied entries lack numerical temperature, pressure, pH, residence-time, catalyst-availability and transfer specifications. Although the overview mentions screening conditions and transport equations, those details are not included here and cannot be credited as validated environmental compatibility. The largest terminal uncertainty is rxn_016; the direct hydrolysis steps rxn_012 and rxn_013 also require explicit operating conditions. The side reactions are chemically appropriate: rxn_017 produces a competing thiol rather than the methylthio precursor, rxn_018 and rxn_019 represent reversible cyanohydrin partitioning rather than an obligatory permanent sink, and rxn_020 is a plausible conditional thermal-decarboxylation channel, not a complete decomposition model or an unavoidable loss on surface-only routes. Anoxia and local UV shielding are reasonable protective assumptions if physically justified. Reaction-local citations and mappings to measured conditions remain missing despite strong support in the supplied research. No problematic_reactions entry denotes a conservation failure; these entries identify operational, kinetic or evidential gaps. Overall confidence reflects the complete network's chemistry and evidence, without rewarding pathway multiplicity, shared intermediates or any particular environmental sequence.
